title: 1 Chronicles 11:1–9
context: All Israel gathers to David at Hebron, recalling that he led Israel even under Saul and that the LORD called him to shepherd his people. The elders make a covenant with David and anoint him king, in keeping with the LORD’s word through Samuel. David and all Israel then take Jebus, the stronghold of Zion, which becomes David’s city; Joab, the first to strike the Jebusites, becomes chief. David builds the city around, Joab repairs the rest, and David grows greater because the LORD of Armies is with him. The parallel is 2 Samuel 5:1–10. Chronicles moves directly from Saul’s death to this anointing, and it includes some details not in Samuel (Joab’s role) while omitting others (David’s age and reign length, and the saying about the blind and the lame).

verses.text: Then all Israel gathered themselves to David to Hebron, saying, “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh.
verses.arminianNotes: All Israel gathers to David at Hebron, claiming kinship as his bone and flesh. Arminian readers note the people’s willing response, coming together to recognize the king God had chosen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the unity of all Israel as a key theme for the Chronicler. Shared ground: the verse parallels 2 Samuel 5:1, and Chronicles moves directly here from Saul’s death, without the years of civil war in 2 Samuel 2–4.

verses.text: In times past, even when Saul was king, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. The LORD your God said to you, ‘You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over my people Israel.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The people recall that David led Israel even under Saul, and that the LORD called him to shepherd his people. Arminian readers see the people recognizing both David’s proven service and God’s call.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shepherd language as rooted in God’s choice of David (compare 1 Samuel 16:11–13). Both traditions read the verse as parallel to 2 Samuel 5:2, with God’s word, not merely popular acclaim, as the ground of David’s rule.

verses.text: So all the elders of Israel came to the king to Hebron; and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the LORD. They anointed David king over Israel, according to the LORD’s word by Samuel.
verses.arminianNotes: The elders make a covenant with David at Hebron and anoint him king, according to the LORD’s word by Samuel. Arminian readers note the covenant between king and people, involving commitments on both sides.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Chronicles adds the phrase “according to the LORD’s word by Samuel,” stressing the fulfillment of God’s promise. Shared ground: the verse parallels 2 Samuel 5:3; Chronicles omits David’s age and reign length in 5:4–5.

verses.text: David and all Israel went to Jerusalem (also called Jebus); and the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, were there.
verses.arminianNotes: David and all Israel go to Jerusalem, called Jebus, where the Jebusites live. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler emphasizes “all Israel” acting together with David from the start of his reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the move to Jerusalem as preparing for the city’s central role in God’s purposes. Both traditions read the verse as parallel to 2 Samuel 5:6, which mentions David and his men rather than all Israel.

verses.text: The inhabitants of Jebus said to David, “You will not come in here!” Nevertheless David took the stronghold of Zion. The same is David’s city.
verses.arminianNotes: The Jebusites say David will not come in, yet he takes the stronghold of Zion. Arminian readers note that Chronicles gives a shorter version of the taunt than 2 Samuel 5:6, without the saying about the blind and lame.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the capture of Zion as a decisive act that God enables. Shared ground: the verse parallels 2 Samuel 5:7, and both traditions read it as the founding of David’s city, while the exact extent of the stronghold is uncertain.

verses.text: David had said, “Whoever strikes the Jebusites first shall be chief and captain.” Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first, and was made chief.
verses.arminianNotes: David promises that whoever strikes the Jebusites first will be chief, and Joab goes up first. Arminian readers note that this detail is not in 2 Samuel 5, though Joab’s leadership is well known from Samuel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Chronicler explaining how Joab came to command David’s army. Both traditions note that 2 Samuel 5:8 has a different, obscure saying about the watercourse, and the two accounts are noted rather than harmonized.

verses.text: David lived in the stronghold; therefore they called it David’s city.
verses.arminianNotes: David lives in the stronghold, which is called David’s city. Arminian readers note that the city’s name honors the king who took it, marking a new chapter in Israel’s history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s city as the place God will choose for his name. Shared ground: the verse parallels 2 Samuel 5:9a, and both traditions read it as establishing Jerusalem as the royal capital.

verses.text: He built the city all around, from Millo even around; and Joab repaired the rest of the city.
verses.arminianNotes: David builds the city around from Millo, and Joab repairs the rest. Arminian readers note that Chronicles adds Joab’s role in repairing the city, not mentioned in 2 Samuel 5:9.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Millo is usually understood as a terraced or filled structure, though its exact nature is uncertain, as the 2 Samuel 5 notes say. Both traditions read the verse as describing the building up of David’s capital.

verses.text: David grew greater and greater, for the LORD of Armies was with him.
verses.arminianNotes: David grows greater and greater, for the LORD of Armies is with him. Arminian readers see God’s presence as the reason for David’s rise, with David responding faithfully in his early reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as the Chronicler’s summary of God’s favor on his chosen king. Shared ground: the verse parallels 2 Samuel 5:10, and both traditions read God’s presence as the decisive factor in David’s success.
